newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Decline in motivation dogs Israeli army.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Decline in motivation dogs Israeli army.

text.p: Ten years ago Adam Cohen volunteered to do an extra year in the army.
Now, like many Israelis, he is looking for ways to avoid his annual call-up for reserve duty.
Long billed by Israelis as the "people's army" and vaunted as one of world's best fighting forces, the Jewish state's military has a motivation problem.
Polls show that over the past 10 years Israelis have grown less eager to serve in the military and that 18-year-old conscripts are less keen to join combat units.
"I was a real Zionist," Cohen, 31, said with a smile. "My commander called me in for a talk and said the unit needed officers and would I put off my plans to study for a year. I agreed."
Cohen now ignores call-up notices, a change in attitude which is growing. Military officials have only recently acknowledged it in public.
Service, once viewed as a sacred duty in a country conceived in war, has lost much of its status. In some circles, draft-dodging has gained legitimacy.

One factor is the growing Western influence in Israel since the 1980s. Many youngsters who once spent their afternoons in ideology-laden youth movements, now hang out at shopping malls or watch MTV. Some want to do what kids in North America or Western Europe do after high school instead of spending three years in uniform.

A recent survey by Tel Aviv's Bar Ilan university found that only 76 percent of non-religious young people wanted to serve in the army after high school compared with 93 percent a decade ago. The figure dropped from 94 percent to 86 percent for religious Jews.

The fact that the drop was smaller among religious Jews is no surprise, analysts say, and can be traced to Israel-PLO peace deals that gave Palestinians control over parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The agreements proved unpopular with most religious Jews who view the West Bank as land God promised to the Jews.

"The recent eruption of violence in the West Bank will probably contribute to that trend," said political sociologist Yoram Peri, referring to clashes which erupted last month killing 15 Israeli soldiers and 60 Palestinians.

"Religious Jews will feel more strongly about the importance of serving because they think Israel should hang on to the land, while the motivation of secular Jews who don't support Israel's presence in the West Bank and Gaza will decline further."
Fresh recruits were not ashamed to tell Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai during a visit last month that they preferred to serve in rear units.
"I don't have the energy for combat service," one recruit told the minister.
Men are drafted at 18 for three years and spend one month a year on reserve duty until 50. Soldiers in combat units spend most of that month away from their families.

One way soldiers evade service is by convincing army psychologists they are mentally unfit for duty. The stigma of such a diagnosis was once a major deterrent and those who did approach army doctors were often turned down.
But many Israelis no longer view this route as a disgrace and the army in recent years has preferred to exempt the "troublemakers".
"I just started ignoring their summonses. The first few times they made a big deal about it but then they just left me alone," Cohen told Reuters.
The army says 17 percent of recruitment-age youngsters this year were not drafted. Some draft-dodgers are jailed for weeks or months. Others slip through the cracks,
Army Chief of Staff Amnon Shahak says a false notion that Israel is no longer threatened has hastened the decline in motivation.
"Today, it's not a shame to dodge service, it's not a shame to say 'This doesn't suit me,'" Shahak said recently on Israel television.

"Maybe for many people there's a feeling that the existential threat no longer exists, that only a few (militants) threaten our border and that's it. Maybe the last war was really a long time ago and a new generation has emerged in Israel thinking there's no great danger," he said.
Israel has fought five wars with Arab neighbours since its creation in 1948 but not since 1973 have the armed forces been fully mobilised.
For all its might, which is believed to include a nuclear arsenal, the army has channeled much of its effort in the last 10 years to suppressing civilian unrest in occupied Arab lands.

A conscript was likely to spend much of his service chasing stone-throwing youths in the West Bank and Gaza Strip or fighting Hizbollah guerrillas beyond Israel's Lebanon border, tasks which tend to erode morale.
Combat soldiers complain they have to shoulder most of the burden in these two areas.

"This deterioration, in terms of the number of draft dodgers and the burden placed on those who do serve is disintegrating the reserve alignment," said Itai Landsberger, a reserve regiment commander who has lobbied the government to give reservists tax incentives and other privileges.
Landsberger said that as long as a small number of soldiers were doing a large amount of the work, the draft-dodging would continue.
